第 86 章 Transparency Takes More Than an Open Door透明不只是一扇开着的门

Seth Dobbs / 塞斯·多布斯

— 第 234 页 —

"I have an open-door policy," is a claim I often hear from managers and leaders. It's a statement that is meant to sound positive and make the speaker seem approachable, but I'm not sure that this is always the case. Don't get me wrong, the intent behind this notion is positive and worth understanding, but my sense is that if you're bragging about the "policy" and not the results, something might be amiss.

「我有开门政策，」是我经常从经理和领导那里听到的说法。这个说法本意听起来积极、让说话者显得平易近人，但我不确定情况总是如此。别误会，这个概念背后的意图是积极的、值得理解的，但我的感觉是如果你在吹嘘「政策」而不是结果，可能哪里不对。

To begin, for many of us in leadership positions, stating, "I have an open door, come in any time!" is easier said than done. Our jobs as leaders and managers often require us to be heads down in a problem, spend time in deep strategic thinking, and to fill our calendars with planned interactions. Given that, how easy is it for your team to actually find time with you? Can people really walk in throughout the day and chat?

首先，对我们很多在领导岗位的人来说，说「我门开着，随时进来！」说起来容易做起来难。我们作为领导和经理的工作经常要求我们埋头问题、花时间深度战略思考、用计划好的互动填满日历。既然如此，你的团队真的容易找到和你在一起的时间吗？人们真的能全天走进来聊天吗？

Also, how comfortable are your people in taking up your time? Role power will naturally make people hesitant to speak to you no matter how much you tout your open door. Even people who are naturally approachable can suffer from this because people on your teams might feel that no matter what you say, you are too busy to actually listen to them. And when you have role power it's really easy to inadvertently imply that you're too busy.

还有，你的人占用你时间有多自在？角色权力自然会让人们犹豫和你说话，不管你怎么吹嘘开门。即使天生平易近人的人也会受此影响，因为你团队的人可能觉得不管你说什么，你太忙了不会真的听他们。当你有角色权力时，很容易不经意地暗示你太忙。

How do you react when people walk in the door and tell you something you don't want to hear? If you are dismissive, unreceptive, or, worse, aggressive, how often do you expect people to come back? Do you actively listen and even empathize? Do you just nod your head, say, "Thanks," and let them walk away? Again, due to role power, people might fear the reaction of their leaders for adverse opinions, so it takes more than just saying you have an open door to get meaningful input.

当人们走进门告诉你不想听的事情时你怎么反应？如果你 dismissive、不接受，或者更糟、有攻击性，你期望人们多久回来一次？你积极倾听甚至共情吗？你只是点头说「谢谢」然后让他们走吗？再说，由于角色权力，人们可能害怕领导对反对意见的反应，所以要获得有意义的输入，光说你开门是不够的。

— 第 235 页 —

I feel that sometimes we encourage feedback on the belief that we're mostly going to hear positive things or minor changes that we already had in mind and the feedback we receive will reinforce it. However, if you're not truly ready to hear contrary opinions and criticism, be careful what you encourage! Given the challenges in actually getting people through your door and having meaningful conversations, I have to wonder what claiming an "open door" actually accomplishes. My fear is that we can have the illusion of knowing what's going on. It's easy to claim, "No one has come in and complained," and therefore assume everything is fine, but that's likely not true. Your teams are always talking about something. That you not hearing it doesn't mean it isn't happening.

我觉得有时候我们鼓励反馈是基于我们主要会听到积极的事或我们心里已经有的小改变、收到的反馈会强化它的信念。然而，如果你没有真正准备好听反对意见和批评，小心你鼓励的东西！考虑到真的让人进门和进行有意义对话的挑战，我不禁想宣称「开门」到底达成了什么。我担心的是我们可能有知道在发生什么的错觉。很容易声称「没人进来抱怨」，因此假设一切都好，但那很可能不是真的。你的团队总在谈论什么。你没听到不意味着它没在发生。

A Better Way更好的方式

If we take a step back and look at why someone might have a positively intentioned open-door policy, I'd say there are a couple key goals: fostering communication and collaboration, and knowing how your people are doing. Again, I'd offer that simply having an open door or talking about having an open door will accomplish these. A good leader doesn't wait for people to come to them. We should actively seek out feedback instead of waiting for it to trickle your way. We need to build trusting relationships so that our people feel like they truly can talk to us. Getting there requires reciprocal transparency. In other words, we can't expect people to tell us everything on their minds if we keep the reasoning behind all of our decision-making a secret. It requires being able to hear things that make us uncomfortable, that might make us question whether we're actually doing a good job.

如果我们退一步看为什么有人会有积极意图的开门政策，我会说有几个关键目标：培养沟通和协作、知道你的人怎么样。再说，我认为光开门或谈论开门就能实现这些。好领导不等人们来找他们。我们应该主动寻求反馈而不是等它 trickle 到你这里。我们需要建立信任关系，让我们的人觉得他们真的可以和我们谈。到达那里需要对等透明。换句话说，如果我们把所有决策背后的理由保密，就不能期望人们告诉我们他们脑子里的一切。它要求能听到让我们不舒服的事情，那些可能让我们质疑自己是否真的在做好工作。

Also, depending on the size of your organization, you might need intermediaries who are trusted and can bring information to you. Then, if you hear of a problem, don't just say, "Let them know they can talk to me." You'll run into the same issues associated with an open door: people think you're too busy (and maybe you are). Instead, seek out the people and let them know you are interested in learning more. Put simply, these are the key ingredients to having open communication across your team:

还有，取决于你组织的大小，你可能需要被信任、能给你带来信息的中间人。然后，如果你听说一个问题，不要只是说「告诉他们可以找我谈。」你会遇到和开门一样的问题：人们觉得你太忙（也许你确实忙）。相反，找到那些人，让他们知道你有兴趣了解更多。简而言之，这些是团队内开放沟通的关键要素：

  • Build relationships建立关系
  • Seek feedback寻求反馈
— 第 236 页 —
  • Develop trust培养信任
  • Be open about mistakes对错误开放
  • Take action!采取行动！

This last point is what makes the relationship really work. If people see that positive changes come from providing feedback, they are more likely to speak up again. This is a good thing. Finally, in an even moderately large organization you'll need intermediaries, so make sure that every team member has a relationship with someone who is trusted and seeking feedback and who will bring to you concerns they can't resolve. If we do this properly, instead of saying, "I have an open-door policy, people can come in any time," we can state that we have a close relationship with our people and can work with mutual transparency to collaborate on even the most difficult issues facing our organization.

最后一点是让关系真正运转的东西。如果人们看到积极改变来自提供反馈，他们更可能再次发声。这是好事。最后，在一个中等大小的组织里你会需要中间人，所以确保每个团队成员和一个被信任、寻求反馈、会把他们无法解决的担忧带给你的人有关系。如果我们做得对，我们可以不说「我有开门政策，人们随时可以进来」，而是说我们和我们的人有亲密关系，可以在相互透明下协作解决组织面临的最困难问题。
